text:
Recent work supports separating item similarity from complementarity. [SComGNN (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28734) models complements through both relevance and dissimilarity, combining low-pass and mid-pass graph filters with attention. This suggests that smoothing all connected items toward similar embeddings can lose useful complementary structure. [DAKSR (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.is.2024.102470) explicitly incorporates item–item knowledge-graph correlations into sequential recommendation, but its external relation information is unavailable here. Neither approach establishes that consecutive interactions alone identify complements or product compatibility.

The no-pretrained-weights constraint excludes prominent text-based approaches such as [WhitenRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10602), which operates on pretrained text embeddings. An older relevant precedent, [Sceptre](https://cs.stanford.edu/people/jure/pubs/prodgraph-kdd15.pdf), learns substitute/complement relationships using product text and topic models, though its original inputs and relation supervision exceed this task’s available evidence. A feasible experimental adaptation—not a verified result from these papers—is to retain SASRec, learn a small token-embedding encoder from available titles/descriptions, and add separately weighted text-match and directed transition scores. Train all parameters from scratch using training histories; preserve item-ID residuals to distinguish near-identical titles. Treat transition edges as behavioral associations and text overlap as content evidence, without asserting compatibility or complement labels. Select fusion weights and graph strength using macro validation HR@10 across all four categories.
